prompt: A cartel has stable demand and high entry barriers. Members meet repeatedly and can punish cheating in future periods. Why may this strengthen cooperation?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeated meetings eliminate members’ gains from additional output.

options.label: B
options.text: High entry barriers make all cartel members price takers.

options.label: C
options.text: Future punishment can outweigh immediate gains from cheating.

options.label: D
options.text: Future punishment necessarily reduces the product price to zero.

explanation: Repeated dealings can make cooperation more sustainable when defection threatens future cartel profits.
reference: 7.7 Growth and Survival of Firms | 7.7.4 cartels: conditions for an effective cartel | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A principal cannot observe a manager’s effort, but can observe profit, which is also affected by random market conditions. What difficulty does this create for incentive pay?

options.label: A
options.text: Observed profit also reflects events outside managers’ control.

options.label: B
options.text: Observed profit cannot be measured in monetary units.

options.label: C
options.text: Observed profit eliminates differences in managers’ preferred objectives.

options.label: D
options.text: Observed profit transfers ownership from shareholders to consumers.

explanation: Observable performance is an imperfect signal of effort, so incentive contracts can expose managers to risks unrelated to their decisions.
reference: 7.7 Growth and Survival of Firms | 7.7.5 principal–agent problem arising from differing objectives of shareholders/owners and managers | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm chooses not to grow even though additional investment has a positive expected return. Which explanation is consistent with 7.7.1?

options.label: A
options.text: Profitable opportunities require the owner to expand internally.

options.label: B
options.text: Every business must choose the greatest possible production scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Owners may value independence more than further expansion.

options.label: D
options.text: Profitable opportunities require acquisition of an existing competitor.

explanation: Firm size is influenced by owner objectives as well as technical and market factors.
reference: 7.7 Growth and Survival of Firms | 7.7.1 reasons for different sizes of firms | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which combination gives the strongest case for external rather than organic growth?1 rapid market entry is valuable2 target has scarce technology3 integration risks are low4 the firm wants to avoid acquiring another organisation

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 4 only; a takeover gives rapid market entry without acquiring another organisation.

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 4 only

options.label: D
options.text: 1, 2 and 3 only

explanation: Rapid entry and access to scarce assets favour acquisition, while wanting to avoid acquiring another organisation favours organic growth.

prompt: A merger is expected to create economies of scale, but it also raises the firm above the scale at which managerial diseconomies begin. What is the safest prediction?

options.label: A
options.text: Scale economies necessarily dominate managerial diseconomies.

options.label: B
options.text: Managerial diseconomies must dominate economies of scale as soon as any coordination difficulties appear within the firm.

options.label: C
options.text: The opposing effects necessarily cancel each other exactly.

options.label: D
options.text: The net cost effect depends on their relative sizes.

explanation: Economies and diseconomies work in opposite directions; without magnitudes, the overall cost effect cannot be known.
reference: 7.7 Growth and Survival of Firms | 7.7.3 external growth of firms – consequences of integration | AO3 Evaluation
